column8: Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the Battle of Bunker Hill, fought on the seventeenth of June 1775, across the river from Boston. In one night, New England soldiers dug an earthen fort on a hill above Charlestown, across the water from Boston. The next afternoon, British soldiers crossed the water to take it. They did, at a terrible cost. We will tell you what is known, who said what, and what is still argued about. Some chapters describe deaths. We tell them plainly and without detail.

Bunker hill, 1775. On the night of the sixteenth of June 1775, about a thousand New England soldiers dug an earthen fort, called a redoubt, on Breed's Hill, on the Charlestown peninsula, across the water from British-held Boston. The next afternoon, British soldiers under General William Howe landed on the peninsula and attacked it. The British were driven back before a final assault took the fort, after the defenders had nearly run out of ammunition. The British won the hill, but more than a thousand of their soldiers were killed or wounded.

A war has begun. Two months earlier, on the nineteenth of April, British soldiers and Massachusetts militia had fought at Lexington and Concord. Since then, thousands of militiamen from all over New England had surrounded Boston, where the British army was based. Boston was then almost an island: a hilly peninsula joined to the mainland only by a narrow neck of land. On this page, the British are red and the New England provincials are blue.

Who is who. On the British side: General Thomas gayj, the governor and commander in Boston; General William Howe, who led the attack; Brigadier Robert pig-ot; and General Henry Clinton. On the provincial side: Colonel William Prescott, who commanded the fort; General Israel Putnam; the engineer Colonel Richard Gridley; Colonels John Stark and James Reed of New Hampshire; Captain Thomas noal-ton of Connecticut; and Doctor Joseph Warren, a leader of Massachusetts, who fought as a volunteer. Many provincials wore their own civilian clothes. There was no standard uniform across the force, and the Stars and Stripes had yet to be adopted.

How this page tells it. Each line is tagged with where it comes from. Some famous words were written down only years later. We tell you which. The maps are painted from maps drawn in 1775 and 1777. Much of today's Boston was water then. The numbers of soldiers and of losses are on screen, in tables, with who counted them.

Boston surrounded. After Lexington and Concord, the New England militia camped in a great half-circle around Boston, from Cambridge to Roxbury. General ar-teh-mas Ward commanded them from Cambridge. Several thousand British troops were stationed in Boston, with the warships of the Royal Navy. In May, three more British generals arrived: Howe, Clinton and bur-goin. The British planned to seize the hills around the town. The provincials learned of it.

Orders to fortify. On the fifteenth of June, the Massachusetts Committee of Safety recommended that the hill called Bunker's Hill, in Charlestown, be "securely kept and defended". Colonel Prescott later wrote that, on the evening of the sixteenth, he received orders to march to Breed's Hill, with a party of about a thousand men. They set out from Cambridge after dark, crossed the narrow Charlestown Neck, and climbed onto the peninsula. Why they built on Breed's Hill, closer to Boston, and not on Bunker Hill behind it, is still argued about.

A fort in one night. About midnight, Prescott wrote, "we began the entrenchment". Through the short summer night they dug a roughly square earthwork, about forty metres across, with earthen walls about as high as a person. Boston was asleep less than a mile away across the water.

Dawn. At daybreak, General gayj wrote, the alarm was given by the guns of the warship Lively. Soon other warships and a battery on kops Hill in Boston were firing at the new fort. The historian Richard froth-ing-ham identifies one man killed in the morning bombardment as Asa Pollard of bill-rick-a. The provincials kept digging. After daybreak, Prescott says, his men extended a breastwork, a low earthen wall, north from the fort while British guns were firing.

The British plan. In Boston, gayj met his generals. According to accounts of the council, Clinton proposed landing behind the fort, at Charlestown Neck, to cut it off. gayj chose instead to land in front of it, at moal-tens Point, and to attack up the hill. Howe would command. Preparing the landing took several hours.

The landing. Early in the afternoon, boats rowed the first British troops across: ten companies of grenadiers, ten of light infantry, and four infantry battalions. They landed unopposed at moal-tens Point. More came after them. Howe later put his strength at about twenty-two hundred rank-and-file soldiers when the attack began.

The rail fence. Meanwhile, more provincials had crossed the Neck under fire from the ships: the New Hampshire men of Colonels Stark and Reed. With noal-ton's Connecticut men, they lined a rail fence, and a stone wall down to the mis-tick River, on the open left of the fort. Joseph Warren arrived, and joined the defenders in the fort as a volunteer.

The first attack. Howe's light infantry advanced along the narrow beach by the mis-tick. His grenadiers advanced on the rail fence. pig-ot's regiments advanced on the fort. The provincials held their fire until the British were close. Then they fired. The attack was driven back, with heavy British losses. "Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" is a famous order. It comes from later accounts. We don't know who, if anyone, said it at Bunker Hill.

Charlestown burns. Provincials fired on the British flank from the houses of Charlestown. During the fighting, British forces set the town on fire. Most of its people had already fled. The fire destroyed much of the town. From Boston, General bur-goin watched Charlestown go up in flames.

The second attack. The British re-formed and attacked again. Again they were driven back. British field guns supported the advance, though their effectiveness varied. The battle is usually told as three attacks. Accounts from different parts of the field count them differently.

The third attack. More British troops crossed to the peninsula. General Clinton followed, and helped rally the troops. The British attacked the fort again, with bayonets. Inside, the powder was nearly gone. Prescott wrote that his men "could keep up only a scattering fire". British soldiers climbed over the walls, and the defenders were forced to retreat. Joseph Warren was killed in the final fighting. British Major John pit-cairn was mortally wounded.

The retreat. The men at the rail fence held long enough to cover the retreat. General Putnam tried to make a stand on Bunker Hill, and could not. The provincials crossed back over Charlestown Neck, under fire from the ships. The British did not follow beyond the Neck.

The cost. The British official return counted two hundred and twenty-six killed and eight hundred and twenty-eight wounded. About four hundred and fifty provincials were killed, wounded, captured or reported missing. Counts from the time differ. You can see them on screen. "The success is too dearly bought," General Howe wrote afterward. General gayj wrote to London that "the rebels are not the despicable rabble too many have supposed them to be". In December, fourteen people, including Colonel Prescott, signed a petition asking Massachusetts to reward Salem Poor, a Black soldier, who they said "behaved like an experienced officer".

Bunker Hill remembered. On the second of July, George Washington arrived at Cambridge to command the new Continental Army. In March 1776, his army fortified Dorchester Heights, and the British left Boston. gayj was recalled to England, and Howe took command. The fighting reached both hills. The fort stood on the one we now call Breed's Hill, and the battle took the name of Bunker Hill. The granite Bunker Hill Monument, dedicated in 1843, stands where the fort was. In 2026, City of Boston archaeologists found part of the fort's ditch, with musket balls and gunflints.

The British held the peninsula, and the siege of Boston went on. More than a thousand British soldiers were killed or wounded. About four hundred and fifty provincials were killed, wounded, captured or reported missing. Charlestown was burned. Why the fort was built on Breed's Hill. A war has begun. Two months earlier, on the nineteenth of April, British soldiers and Massachusetts militia had fought at Lexington and Concord. Since then, thousands of militiamen from all over New England had surrounded Boston, where the British army was based. Boston was then almost an island: a hilly peninsula joined to the mainland only by a narrow neck of land. On this page, the British are red and the New England provincials are blue.

Who is who. On the British side: General Thomas gayj, the governor and commander in Boston; General William Howe, who led the attack; Brigadier Robert pig-ot; and General Henry Clinton. On the provincial side: Colonel William Prescott, who commanded the fort; General Israel Putnam; the engineer Colonel Richard Gridley; Colonels John Stark and James Reed of New Hampshire; Captain Thomas noal-ton of Connecticut; and Doctor Joseph Warren, a leader of Massachusetts, who fought as a volunteer. Many provincials wore their own civilian clothes. There was no standard uniform across the force, and the Stars and Stripes had yet to be adopted.

Dawn. At daybreak, General gayj wrote, the alarm was given by the guns of the warship Lively. Soon other warships and a battery on kops Hill in Boston were firing at the new fort. After daybreak, Prescott says, his men extended a breastwork, a low earthen wall, north from the fort while British guns were firing.

The British plan. In Boston, gayj met his generals. According to accounts of the council, Clinton proposed landing behind the fort, at Charlestown Neck, to cut it off. gayj chose instead to land in front of it, at moal-tens Point, and to attack up the hill. Howe would command. Preparing the landing took several hours.

The landing. Early in the afternoon, boats rowed the first British troops across: ten companies of grenadiers, ten of light infantry, and four infantry battalions. They landed unopposed at moal-tens Point. More came after them. Howe later put his strength at about twenty-two hundred rank-and-file soldiers when the attack began.

The rail fence. Meanwhile, more provincials had crossed the Neck under fire from the ships: the New Hampshire men of Colonels Stark and Reed. With noal-ton's Connecticut men, they lined a rail fence, and a stone wall down to the mis-tick River, on the open left of the fort. Joseph Warren arrived, and joined the defenders in the fort as a volunteer.

The first attack. Howe's light infantry advanced along the narrow beach by the mis-tick. His grenadiers advanced on the rail fence. pig-ot's regiments advanced on the fort. The provincials held their fire until the British were close. Then they fired. The attack was driven back, with heavy British losses. "Don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" is a famous order. It comes from later accounts. We don't know who, if anyone, said it at Bunker Hill.

Charlestown burns. Provincials fired on the British flank from the houses of Charlestown. During the fighting, British forces set the town on fire. Most of its people had already fled. The fire destroyed much of the town. From Boston, General bur-goin watched Charlestown go up in flames.
